strengths: Novel combination of techniques tailored to real gaps in V2A: masked flow-matching for audio conditioning/outpainting and long-form generation, and shortcut-loss training for native few-step sampling without a separate distillation stage — the paper is (to its knowledge) first to apply shortcut models in the audio generation domain.

Custom contrastive audio-visual synchronization model built on a larger pretrained backbone (VideoPrism) with a sensible batch-size ablation rationale (avoiding dilution of hard negatives), motivated by observed failure modes of Synchformer-based sync features used in prior work.

Strong empirical results: outperforms MMAudio (a larger, 1.03B-parameter SOTA model) on several objective metrics and on synchronization/DeSync despite having ~40% fewer parameters, and wins on human-rated overall quality and synchronization in a listening study.

Convincing few-step sampling and long-form generation experiments (Figure 5), showing graceful degradation compared to MMAudio's sharp performance drop at low sampling budgets and beyond ~20s duration.

Reasonably thorough reproducibility details in the appendix (architecture dimensions, training hyperparameters, framework/hardware, masked inference procedure, and a new SWSD metric with pseudocode for assessing conditional spectral fidelity).
Honest limitations section that acknowledges the audio-quality MOS gap relative to MMAudio and discusses failure modes of the outpainting-based long-form approach (scene cuts).
weaknesses: Missing comparisons to the most relevant specialized baselines: V-AURA (designed for long-form/autoregressive generation) is discussed at length in related work but never empirically compared against for the long-form experiments, and Frieren (the only other V2A model with dedicated few-step sampling via reflow) is never compared against in the few-step sampling experiments — both omissions weaken the two central claimed contributions (long-form and fast sampling).

The long-form comparison against MMAudio may not be entirely apples-to-apples: MMAudio processes the full un-chunked sequence while SALSA-V uses a 10-second rolling context, and the paper's own explanation attributes part of MMAudio's mid-range advantage to this difference in setup rather than isolating the true underlying capability gap.

Human MOS study reveals SALSA-V is rated lower than MMAudio on audio quality (2.96 vs 3.16), undercutting the abstract's blanket claim that the model "significantly outperforms" prior work; this is disclosed but somewhat downplayed relative to its prominence in the abstract.

The human evaluation is based on only 10 videos and 18 participants (180 total ratings), which is a fairly small sample for drawing statistically robust conclusions, and no significance testing (e.g., confidence intervals, p-values) is reported for the MOS differences.

The contribution of the custom VideoPrism-based synchronization model is not isolated via ablation — there is no controlled comparison substituting Synchformer sync features into the same generative pipeline to confirm that synchronization gains stem from this component specifically, rather than other architectural or training choices.
The DeSync metric is described as having a resolution of 0.2 seconds, yet results are reported to three decimal places (e.g., 0.497), which is inconsistent/unclear and not explained.
The text encoder used for text conditioning is not clearly specified in the main text, limiting reproducibility of that conditioning pathway.

Long-form evaluation only extends to 60 seconds; given the chunked-outpainting mechanism could accumulate drift or degrade coherence over much longer durations (minutes), the claimed "unconstrained length" capability is not empirically substantiated beyond this modest range.

strengths: The paper combines several individually interesting ideas into one coherent system: a masked flow-matching objective enabling audio conditioning and chunked long-form generation, a shortcut-loss formulation (novel in the V2A/audio domain) for native few-step sampling without distillation, and a custom contrastively-trained synchronization model built on a larger pretrained video backbone (VideoPrism) than prior Synchformer-based approaches.

The shortcut-loss ablation (Table 2) is a useful sanity check, showing that the shortcut objective does not degrade performance at full sampling budgets relative to vanilla flow matching, which is a meaningful and testable claim.

Reasonably thorough set of objective metrics (FAD, KL-PANNs/PaSST, IS, ImageBind, DeSync) plus a human listening study, and additional analyses of long-form behavior and audio-conditioning fidelity (SWSD) in the appendix.
The qualitative spectrogram examples (impact sounds, outpainting, few-step generation) are illustrative and support the narrative of improved temporal precision.
weaknesses: The human evaluation is very small and underpowered: only 18 participants rating 10 videos each in a single run (180 total scores, ~60 per model per axis), with no reported confidence intervals, variance, or significance tests. The headline claim in the abstract that the model 'significantly outperforms' SOTA in synchronization and alignment is not statistically substantiated given this sample size.

The paper's own results undercut its central claim: SALSA-V scores lower than MMAudio on human-rated 'Quality' (2.96 vs. 3.16) and loses on KL-PANNs and IS, yet the abstract and conclusion present the method as uniformly superior. This is acknowledged only briefly in the Limitations paragraph, which somewhat downplays a core weakness rather than contextualizing it against the 'significantly outperforms' framing in the abstract.

Comparisons are limited to only two baselines (MMAudio, FoleyCrafter), despite the related work section extensively discussing Frieren, V-AURA, Diff-Foley, and LoVA as directly relevant competitors (particularly for few-step sampling and long-form generation, which are the paper's main selling points). Omitting Frieren (the only other few-step V2A model) and LoVA/V-AURA (the only other long-form approaches) from quantitative comparison is a significant evidentiary gap.

The long-form comparison against MMAudio beyond its trained context length is somewhat of a strawman (MMAudio was not designed/trained for that regime), and the explanation for its degradation is speculative ('we hypothesize') rather than empirically isolated.

Model size is confounded with method: SALSA-V (643M) is compared against MMAudio (1.03B), making it hard to attribute performance differences to the proposed techniques versus architecture/capacity differences; the paper acknowledges this only as a 'limitation' explaining its own underperformance on quality, which does not resolve the confound for the metrics it does win on.

The improvement from the newly proposed VideoPrism-based synchronization model is not directly ablated in isolation (e.g., swapping in Synchformer features in the same architecture) — its claimed advantage over Synchformer-based conditioning is inferred indirectly rather than demonstrated via a controlled comparison.

Reproducibility is limited: training relies on a proprietary 'high-fidelity studio Foley' dataset that is not described in detail or released, and no code/model/sample link is functional in the provided manuscript (placeholder only), making independent verification of audio quality claims impossible.

Several objective metric differences (e.g., FAD 1.07 vs. 1.12, DeSync 0.497 vs 0.521) are small and not accompanied by variance estimates or significance testing, so it is unclear whether reported gains are meaningful or within noise.

strengths: Combines several well-motivated techniques into a coherent system: a masked flow-matching objective that simultaneously enables audio-conditioned generation, outpainting, and long-form synthesis via iterative extension; and a shortcut-loss objective that is, to the authors' knowledge, the first application of this few-step sampling technique to the audio/V2A domain. The combination addresses several practical limitations of prior V2A work (short context, slow sampling, text-only control) in a unified framework.

The new contrastively-trained synchronization model built on a larger pretrained video backbone (VideoPrism) plus a fine-tuned AST audio encoder is a reasonable technical contribution, and the resulting DeSync numbers and qualitative spectrogram comparisons (Figure 3) support the claim of improved temporal alignment relative to Synchformer-based conditioning used in prior works.

The evaluation is fairly comprehensive: multiple distribution-matching and semantic-alignment metrics (FAD, KL variants, IS, ImageBind), a dedicated DeSync synchronization metric, a human listening study with three separately rated axes, and additional quantitative probes for audio-conditioning fidelity (SWSD) and long-form behavior (FAD/DeSync vs. duration).

Ablations isolate the effect of the shortcut objective versus vanilla flow matching at matched model sizes (Table 2), supporting the claim that shortcut training does not sacrifice full-step fidelity, and the few-step sampling comparison against MMAudio (Fig. 5) is a convincing demonstration of relative robustness to reduced sampling budgets.

Reasonably strong reproducibility effort: extensive appendix detailing architecture, training hyperparameters, VAE fine-tuning procedure, contrastive pretraining setup, and the human-evaluation interface/protocol.

SALSA-V achieves competitive or best-in-class results in several objective and subjective measures while using notably fewer parameters (643M) than the main baseline MMAudio (1.03B), suggesting reasonable efficiency.
weaknesses: The human listening study is small (18 participants, only 10 videos), and no statistical significance testing (e.g., confidence intervals, p-values) is reported for the MOS differences, which are sometimes narrow (e.g., Overall 3.43 vs 3.29). This limits confidence in the human-evaluation conclusions.

The paper's own results show SALSA-V trailing MMAudio on the 'Quality' axis of the human study (2.96 vs 3.16) and on KL_PANNs, which is acknowledged in the Limitations section but is not further analyzed (e.g., failure-mode examples, variance across samples) beyond attributing it to parameter count.

Table 1 and the accompanying text use 'Overall' and 'Quality' columns in a way that is easy to conflate (the text's claim of leading 'overall quality' actually refers to the 'Overall' axis, not the 'Quality'/fidelity axis), which is a presentation issue that could mislead readers skimming the results.

Direct quantitative comparison against Frieren and V-AURA—two of the most relevant prior works specifically targeting few-step sampling and long-form/autoregressive generation, respectively—is missing from the main results table; these are only discussed qualitatively in related work, weakening the claims of state-of-the-art status in those specific sub-problems.

The contrastive synchronization model is trained with a very small batch size (28–30) due to the hard-negative argument; while plausible, this choice is not rigorously ablated (e.g., via a sweep of batch sizes with corresponding sync retrieval or downstream V2A metrics) beyond a reference to a similar finding in Synchformer, leaving open questions about robustness and scalability of this design choice.

Long-form evaluation extends only to 60 seconds, and the iterative-outpainting approach's potential for drift/error accumulation or audio consistency degradation over much longer sequences (minutes) is not empirically examined, despite 'unconstrained length' being an abstract-level claim.

No discussion of dataset licensing, consent, or ethical considerations around the use of in-the-wild YouTube data (via Panda70M) and a proprietary 'high-fidelity studio Foley' dataset, nor broader-impact discussion of risks (e.g., misuse for fabricating synchronized audio for manipulated videos).

The audio sample link referenced in the abstract/intro is redacted/not provided in the reviewed manuscript, so the central qualitative claims about audio fidelity and synchronization cannot be independently verified by the reviewer.

Several core components (SigLIP2 visual encoder, VideoPrism backbone, AST, Stable-Audio VAE) are pretrained/off-the-shelf, so much of the contribution lies in integration and the two training-objective modifications (masking, shortcut) rather than fundamentally new architectures or theory; the originality is therefore moderate rather than high.

strengths: The paper combines three well-motivated technical contributions (shortcut loss for native few-step sampling, masked flow matching enabling both audio conditioning and iterative long-form extension, and a new large-backbone contrastive synchronization model) into a coherent system, and is the first to apply shortcut models to the video-to-audio/general audio generation domain.

Extensive comparison against a wide range of recent baselines (Frieren, V-AURA, LoVA, AudioX, FoleyCrafter, MMAudio) across multiple standard objective metrics (FAD, KL divergence with two classifiers, IS, ImageBind, DeSync) plus a human listening study, giving a fairly complete picture of performance.

Dedicated experiments targeting each claimed capability: few-step generation vs. Frieren-reflow and MMAudio at reduced steps (Table 3, Fig. 4), long-form generation vs. MMAudio and LoVA (Table 5, Fig. 4), and audio-conditioning fidelity via a custom Sliced-Wasserstein Spectral Distance metric (Section A.3) with qualitative spectrogram evidence (Figs. 3, 5, 8, 9).
Reasonably detailed appendix with training hyperparameters, architecture specifics, VAE fine-tuning, and pseudocode for the proposed SWSD metric, aiding partial reproducibility.

Ablation isolating the effect of the shortcut objective versus vanilla flow matching at matched model size, and a model-scaling study (347M/643M/1.01B), supporting the claim that shortcut training does not compromise full-step fidelity.
weaknesses: The human listening study is small (10 videos, 18 participants, 180 total ratings) with no reported statistical significance or variance, and results are mixed: SALSA-V actually scores lower than MMAudio on "Quality" (2.96 vs 3.16) while the text emphasizes the "Overall" win, softening the strength of the human-evaluation claim.

The long-form comparison against MMAudio is confounded: the paper itself attributes MMAudio's degradation beyond ~20s to out-of-distribution positional embeddings rather than an inherent modeling limitation, and SALSA-V's own chunked/iterative approach is only tested up to 60 seconds, leaving open how error/drift accumulates over much longer (minutes-scale) sequences that would better demonstrate the "unconstrained length" claim in the abstract.

The paper's own limitations note that the outpainting-based long-form mechanism struggles with scene cuts/major content changes, but no quantitative analysis of this failure mode (e.g., frequency or magnitude of drift, need for re-seeding) is provided.

Table 2 shows the shortcut variant is occasionally slightly worse than the flow-matching baseline at equal size (e.g., 347M FADVGG 1.12 vs 1.09, IB 31.09 vs 31.21), which is a minor but real caveat against the strong claim of "no performance reduction."
Reproducibility is limited by the absence of a released project page/code/checkpoints (the project page link is left blank), despite fairly detailed textual descriptions of hyperparameters.

Results are not uniformly state-of-the-art across all metrics (e.g., AudioX wins on KLPANNs, MMAudio wins on IS), which is acknowledged but could be discussed more critically regarding when/why SALSA-V underperforms.

Training data composition (~900h audio-visual, ~8.5k h audio-text) differs from baselines, and no controlled comparison isolating the effect of data scale/curation versus architectural/objective contributions is provided, making it harder to attribute performance gains specifically to the proposed methodology.

strengths: The paper tackles several genuinely important open problems in V2A generation simultaneously (long-form generation, audio conditioning/outpainting, few-step sampling), and the architectural choices (MMDiT-X hybrid blocks, masked flow matching, shortcut loss) are reasonably well motivated and clearly described.

Broad empirical evaluation against many recent baselines (Frieren, V-AURA, LoVA, AudioX, FoleyCrafter, MMAudio) across multiple axes: objective distribution-matching metrics, synchronization (DeSync), few-step sampling, long-form generation, and a human listening study.

The ablation isolating the shortcut objective from vanilla flow matching (Table 2) is a useful and appropriately controlled comparison, showing the shortcut loss does not degrade full-step quality while enabling much faster sampling — a meaningful practical contribution given the near-real-time application.

Qualitative analyses (spectrogram visualizations, audio-conditioning experiments, few-step degradation study) are helpful for interpreting where the model succeeds and add plausibility to the quantitative claims.
The paper is candid about a real limitation (scene-cut handling in the outpainting-based long-form approach) rather than hiding it.
weaknesses: The human evaluation is small and likely underpowered: only 10 videos rated by 18 participants (180 total ratings per axis), with no reported variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests, making the claimed superiority in 'overall quality' and 'sync' difficult to trust as robust rather than noise, especially since the quality gap versus MMAudio is small and reversed on the 'Quality' axis (2.96 vs 3.16).

No error bars, standard deviations, or statistical significance tests are reported anywhere in the objective-metric tables (Tables 1, 2, 3, 5, 6), yet several comparisons rest on very small numeric differences (e.g., FADVGG 1.07 vs 1.11 vs 1.12), making it hard to assess whether reported improvements are meaningful.

The training data for the non-VGGSound portion is filtered using the paper's own synchronization model, and evaluation partly relies on both this model's outputs (as conditioning) and a related SynchFormer-based DeSync metric; this creates a risk of circularity/selection bias favoring the proposed pipeline that is not discussed or controlled for.

The long-form comparison against MMAudio is somewhat confounded: MMAudio was not designed or trained for extended-context inputs and predictably degrades on out-of-distribution positional embeddings, while SALSA-V uses an autoregressive chunked-extension procedure suited to this regime; the paper acknowledges this asymmetry but does not attempt a fairer comparison (e.g., chunked/sliding-window inference for MMAudio) to isolate the actual algorithmic contribution.

No code, model weights, or dataset release is provided (the project page link is empty), and the pipeline is complex (custom fine-tuned VAE, custom large-scale contrastive sync model built on VideoPrism, custom filtered ~900h/~8.5k h datasets), which raises significant reproducibility concerns for a paper whose central claims depend heavily on these components.

Individual technical components (shortcut models, masked/inpainting diffusion objectives, MMDiT-style architectures, SigLIP-style contrastive losses) are all adapted from existing work rather than newly proposed; the contribution is primarily integrative/engineering, which is acceptable but somewhat limits originality, and the paper does not include an ablation isolating the contribution of the new synchronization model versus reusing an existing one (e.g., Synchformer) within the same architecture.

Some claims of outperformance are overstated relative to the actual mixed results — e.g., AudioX beats SALSA-V on KLPANNs, MMAudio is competitive or better on IS and human 'Quality', yet the abstract/results text emphasizes broad superiority without fully acknowledging this mixed picture.

The masked flow-matching context used for outpainting during long-form generation is quite short (up to 2.5s during training, and as little as 0.5s used at inference for 9.5s of new generation), raising questions about how well global coherence/semantic drift is maintained over many chained extensions beyond what is shown in the single qualitative example (Figure 5) and the DeSync/FAD curves up to 60s.

strengths: The paper tackles three practically important limitations of V2A models simultaneously (synchronization quality, long-form generation, and slow sampling) and provides a coherent architecture (MMDiT-X + DiT hybrid) and training recipe (masked flow matching + shortcut loss) to address them jointly.

Extensive quantitative comparison against a wide range of recent baselines (Frieren, V-AURA, LoVA, AudioX, FoleyCrafter, MMAudio) across multiple metric families (distribution matching, semantic alignment, temporal synchronization, inference speed), plus a dedicated human listening study with a described blind/randomized web interface.

The few-step generation results (Table 3, Figure 4) are compelling: SALSA-V retains near-full quality down to 8 steps and clearly outperforms both MMAudio and Frieren's reflow-distilled model at 4 steps, without requiring any separate distillation stage, which is a meaningful practical advantage over rectified-flow reflowing.

Long-form evaluation (Figure 4, Table 5) convincingly shows degradation of competing methods beyond their training context length (~20s) while SALSA-V's chunked, mask-conditioned extension approach maintains stable FAD/DeSync up to 60s, addressing a documented gap in prior work.

Reasonable ablations are included: model-size scaling (Table 2, Table 6), flow-matching vs. shortcut objective at equal size (Table 2, showing no fidelity loss from the shortcut objective at full sampling steps), and quantitative analysis of audio-conditioning fidelity via a custom Sliced-Wasserstein Spectral Distance metric with an appendix algorithm.

The paper is transparent about a genuine limitation (autoregressive outpainting struggling with scene cuts) rather than hiding it, and the Impact Statement reasonably discusses dual-use/misinformation risks.
weaknesses: The human listening study is small (18 participants, only 10 videos, 3 methods), with no reported variance, confidence intervals, or significance testing on the MOS differences; the overall-quality gap actually favors MMAudio (3.16 vs 2.96) and the improvement in overall/sync scores for SALSA-V could plausibly be within noise given the sample size.

Objective results are mixed rather than uniformly dominant: AudioX beats SALSA-V on KL_PANNs, and MMAudio matches or exceeds SALSA-V on IS and IB in Table 1, undercutting the strength of the headline 'significantly outperforms' claim in the abstract.

The project page link is left blank in the manuscript, and there is no mention of code or model-weight release; given the substantial engineering complexity of the pipeline (custom VAE fine-tuning, custom contrastive sync model, custom architecture), this raises real reproducibility concerns beyond what the appendix's hyperparameter listing can compensate for.

Some training data (a 'high-fidelity studio Foley set') is not clearly identified as public or proprietary, and exact composition/size of the ~8.5k hours text-audio corpus is not broken down, making it hard for others to reproduce the exact training distribution.

The long-form comparison against MMAudio is somewhat confounded: MMAudio is evaluated in a regime (positional embeddings beyond its training length) that the authors acknowledge is out-of-distribution for it, which is an expected failure mode rather than a fully controlled ablation isolating the contribution of the masked/outpainting mechanism itself.

No ablation is provided for key design choices within the masked flow-matching objective itself (e.g., masking probability, mask length distribution, effect of the two learned mask-state tokens, or importance of the CFG formulation for conditioning) despite these being central to two of the three claimed contributions.

The technical novelty is primarily an integration of existing techniques (shortcut models from image generation, masked/inpainting flow matching akin to VampNet-style tokens, MMDiT-X architecture, SigLIP2/VideoPrism backbones) rather than a fundamentally new modeling idea; the main new element is the larger-backbone contrastive sync model, whose benefit over Synchformer-style sync features is asserted via hypothesis but not directly ablated (e.g., no controlled comparison of SALSA-V with Synchformer features swapped in versus the proposed sync model, both trained end-to-end in the same pipeline).

The claimed 'near-real-time' framing is somewhat generous given reported timings are for batch size 1 offline generation on an A100, not a streaming/interactive setting, and the paper does not discuss latency in a genuinely interactive (partial-video, streaming) use case.
